title: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. v. Jordan International Co.
summary: An expressly conditional acknowledgment followed by performance created a § 2-207(3) contract without the seller’s unmatched arbitration clause.
notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1977).

The shared factual motif with Dorton is insufficient to equate the outcomes. The wording and function of the condition determine which statutory route is used.

sections.Parties: Itoh, the buyer of steel coils, sued Jordan, the seller, alleging defective and late goods. Jordan sought arbitration.
sections.Material Facts: Itoh sent a purchase order. Jordan’s acknowledgment explicitly conditioned its acceptance on the buyer’s assent to additional or different terms, including arbitration. The parties delivered, received, and paid for the steel without obtaining the required assent to that term.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied Jordan’s motion to stay proceedings pending arbitration. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: When the writings fail to form a contract because acceptance is expressly conditional, does later performance adopt the seller’s arbitration clause or form a contract under § 2-207(3)?
sections.Holding: The contract arose by the parties’ conduct under subsection (3). Its terms included the writings’ agreed terms and the Code’s supplementary terms; arbitration was not one of them.
sections.Reasoning: The condition kept subsection (1) from completing a contract through the exchanged writings. Performance nevertheless recognized a sale. Treating delivery and payment as automatic assent to the conditional form would restore the last-shot advantage the provision addresses. A disputed additional term cannot reenter as a “supplementary term” when the Code’s gap-fillers do not supply it. A seller can protect its insistence on arbitration by securing assent before delivery; choosing to perform without it carries the corresponding risk.
